vignette:
He is 24 years old, a painter, and he has been living with his girlfriend for the past fourteen months. They met at a gallery opening where she admired his work, and he remembers feeling seen in a way he rarely did. The first time she hit him was a Tuesday. They had been arguing about a piece he was preparing for a group show, and she said it was derivative. He defended it. She slapped him across the face, hard enough that his ear rang. She apologized immediately, cried, said she was under a lot of pressure at work, that she loved him, that it wouldn’t happen again.

He believed her. He believed her for months.

He describes the pattern now with a hollow calm. She would get tense, he would try to soothe her, and then something small would set her off. A dish left in the sink. A text he didn’t respond to fast enough. The wrong tone. He would find himself pinned against the wall by her forearm, her fist connecting with his ribs, his back. He learned to curl into a ball on the floor. He stopped painting in the living room because that was where she usually came for him. He moved his easel into the bedroom closet, but she found him there, knocked over his canvas, and told him he was wasting his talent on garbage.

He does not talk about the injuries. He says she stopped hitting him three months ago, after he went to the emergency room for three cracked ribs and lied about falling down stairs. But he cannot shake the feeling that she is always about to explode. He watches her hands even when she is smiling. When she reaches up to brush her hair away from her face, he flinches. He has stopped cooking with her because the sound of a knife on a cutting board makes his chest tighten. He cannot eat food she has prepared—he is not sure why, he just knows he cannot swallow it.

At night, he lies awake listening to her breathing. Sometimes he dreams that he is back on the floor of the closet, paint smeared across the concrete, her face blurring above him. He wakes up drenched in sweat, ears ringing. He has started sleeping on the far edge of the mattress, as far from her as possible, but she reaches for him in her sleep and he freezes, pretending to be already asleep.

His painting has changed. He used to work in bold, vibrant colors—yellows, oranges, deep blues. Now he finds himself mixing everything to gray. He cannot hold a brush without his hands trembling. He paints only during the day, when she is at her office, and even then he stops the second he hears a key in the lock. He has lost two commissions because he missed deadlines, and his dealer has stopped calling. His friends think he has become distant. He tells them work is busy. He does not tell anyone that he has started checking the locks twice before bed, or that he feels a constant pressure like a hand around his throat, even when she is not in the room.

He tries to remember what it felt like to be excited about a blank canvas. He tries to remember what it felt like to trust someone. But mostly he thinks about the way her face looked the first time she hit him—surprised, then angry, then ashamed. He feels that sequence loop inside him, over and over, like a song he cannot turn off.
